Mr. Speaker, a couple of days ago the hon. member for Peel inquired about the regrettable aircraft accident which happened near Brampton on February 5 last. Specifically, he asked whether the pilots who were killed were practising forced landings.
In reply I would point out that these two officers were members of the Royal Canadian Air Force primary reserve carrying out training in an aircraft owned by the R.C.A.F. but on loan to, and operated by, the Toronto Flying Club under civilian licence.
As the aircraft is under civilian licence, the investigation of the accident is being carried out by the Department of Transport. However, preliminary information indicates that the officers concerned were practising forced landings for which they had been duly authorized in accordance with the refresher flying training plan in which they were participating.
For the information of hon. members perhaps I might add that the refresher flying training plan is designed to maintain a pool of approximately 600 primary reserve officers as basic flying instructors who can be available in an emergency to assist in the rapid expansion of air force training capacity.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Friday, February 3, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Howe (Port Arthur)- Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, by way of a guarantee for bank loans made on or after the 15th day of November, 1955, and before the 1st day of June, 1956, for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver their grain; to provide also that the governor in council may extend the application of the act to cover loans made before the 1st day of June, 1957; and to provide further that any amount paid to a bank under the act be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
When this debate was adjourned I was dealing with the reasons why we were opposing this legislation as a' means of correcting a very serious cash shortage situation in the prairie regions. At that time I pointed out the scheme was impracticable as a measure to get cash into the hands of the farmers who needed it most.
I maintain it was unjust and wrong in principle to ask those people who had spent their time during the year in producing grain and then, because of the policies of this government, were unable to deliver it, to assume a further burden of debt, and to carry on top of that a further interest of 5 per cent on the loan.
The Manitoba farmer who blasted his television set in a moment of righteous indignation expressed the feelings of the prairie farmers in a very real manner. What he is reported to have said on that occasion exemplifies exactly what the producer thinks. He is reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of February 3 as having said:
That man Tucker! Does he think I am going to work all year and then pay interest to the banks on my whole summer's work?
That is exactly how the farmer looks at this legislation. For that reason we maintain it is unjust and wrong. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) says that he is supporting it, and that the legislation does
(Mr. Harris.]
exactly what it was intended to do. Well, a few farmers may be compelled to pay the 5 per cent interest. A very small percentage of the farmers may be able to qualify. Under the pressure of debts against them they may go to the banks and, if they qualify, assume an extra burden of debt, but I can assure the minister and those who are supporting this legislation that the farmers do so with a great deal of disgust, and they feel the injustice of it.
The difficulties of the situation are very real. I have a letter from one of the producers in my own constituency. He writes:
On January 11, 1956, we delivered our first load of grain since December 22, 1954.
It is over a year since he had been allowed to deliver any grain at all. Many farmers are in the same position, particularly if they had decided that they were not going to deliver the grain except to an elevator which they owned. The farmers' requests have been very clear. If the minister or anybody else assumes that the farmer has been asking for anything else, he is entirely wrong. They made their requests very clear. They asked for cash advances on the grain which is properly stored on the farm. It could be inspected by people who know how to inspect it. It could be graded; it could be sealed up and the advance noted in their permit books so that they would be absolutely sure that they could not deliver without repaying the advance which they had obtained. Surely there is a minimum of justice in their request.
For anyone to agree with this legislation is to agree with what the leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan termed it. It is something useless, as he described it. It is like voting for a stirrup pump in fighting a forest fire. As a matter of fact, the producers there look upon it as a deliberate insult. It reveals a callous disregard for those people who have been placed in the difficulties in which they find themselves today by the policies and the administration of the government opposite. The failure to sell the grain, the failure to provide the means for transporting this grain out of the elevators, have been the two things which have brought about the situation that exists at the present time. Here they are with their bins loaded. Many of them have not even room in their bins for all the wheat. They are still sitting there completely unable to get anything in the way of money to carry on their businesses or to pay any of the cost of operation of the past year.
I was speaking the other day of the difficulty that a person from the prairie region has in letting the people of eastern Canada know what some of the difficulties are out there. I went to the net farm income of the

dominion bureau of statistics and found that the reports for the past three years gave the net farm income in 1954 as compared with 1952. The figures for 1955 are not out yet but the trend is exactly the same. The following are the decreases in net farm income for the eastern provinces from 1952 to 1954:
Maritime provinces	
19	per	centQuebec	
3	per	centOntario	
15	per	cent
When we come to the prairie provinces we find these figures:
Manitoba	
54	per	centSaskatchewan	
77	per	centAlberta	
50	per	centBritish Columbia	
10	per	cent
Those figures reveal why it is the farmers in the west are disturbed about the situation when after another year of decrease in their income they find themselves with an abundant crop of good grain which they are unable to deliver.
It is in the face of the unqualified refusal on the part of the government to give consideration to the payment of cash advances against properly stored farm grain that we make the protest we are making. We are going to continue to make that protest.
To add insult to this refusal to make cash advances on properly stored farm grain, similar to what has been done in the United States for years, we have the Minister of Trade and Commerce saying that those people who recommend such cash advances are enemies of the wheat board method of delivering grain. Then we have the Minister of Agriculture who comes from that area, and who should know what the situation is, saying that the bank loan system will do what it was intended to do. What it is intended to do is to put the producer deeper into debt. It must be that because that is exactly what is going to happen, there will be another burden of interest placed upon his back.
What do we suggest should be done under the circumstances? We say that the farmers should be given advances on properly stored farm grain. This job is too big for the banks to handle and we suggest that since the elevator agents under the arrangement proposed by the government are going to be asked to collect the grain and thus pay off the loan they should be allowed to recommend the advances.
The elevator agent is the one who knows the farmer well. There are far more of these agents throughout the west than there are bankers. Many farmers are some distance away from the bank and they possibly cannot get out to the bank, but all farmers haul their grain to the local elevators. They know the
Crain
elevator agents personally because they do business with them. The elevator agents know the farmers and they could even visit the farms to grade the grain and see that it is properly stored. If necessary they could place seals upon the granary doors. They could enter the details in the permit book which is in the elevator, and when the farmer is allowed to deliver his grain, that could be deducted from the cash advance. The producer would thus be enabled to carry on his operations.
Next I would suggest to the minister that he get his box cars into operation and clear up the congestion that exists. Box cars should be placed across Canada to do the job they are intended to do, that is to carry grain from the small delivery points to the space available in the elevators.
On Monday of this week the house had the privilege of listening to Sir Anthony Eden, Prime Minister of Great Britain. Sir Anthony made a statement which should have been listened to closely by the members of this house when he said:
Economic weapons may take the place of military ones. But always our purpose must be the same; to maintain the right that men's minds may be free and the care that their bellies be filled.
Sir Anthony told the government and this country that the economic weapons of today may replace military weapons. We have a government here which is ready to spend $2,000 million a year on defence and military weapons, but not one-tenth of that for economic production. This government is ready to administer the affairs of this country so that money is spent on military weapons to provide profits for industry in the heavily industrialized areas where prosperity is maintained, but little is spent on those who are producing the economic weapon of food for a hungry world. While the rest of Canada enjoys prosperity, agriculture, which represents about 20 per cent of the population of Canada, must be satisfied with slightly over 8 per cent of the national income.
The government is sponsoring this resolution and the bill to follow, and the official opposition have declared that they are going to support it. The Social Credit party have indicated that they are going to support it, although somewhat reluctantly. The 23 members of this party cannot hope to prevent the passage of the legislation, but we do urge the opposition parties to support us in our fight against a piece of injustice, a piece of useless legislation which will accomplish little more than to add an increased debt burden to those who are doing this job of producing. We oppose it in principle and it is clearly our duty to fight against it. Certainly I can say to the committee that we will never support it.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise to deal with a matter which I attempted to place before the house on an earlier occasion this week, but as it was pointed out to me that there would be another opportunity, I am availing myself of this opportunity as 1 indicated I would. In the Winnipeg Free Press of February 3 was an article on the editorial page dealing with the debate in the house on this subject. It was headed "Farm Loans Debate at Ottawa" and then followed in capitals, "One Solution Overlooked". The article then went on to suggest that the solution overlooked was the proposal for the payment of cash for wheat actually on farms.
I started to point out earlier that this was entirely contrary to the facts. As it was indicated at that time that I could not proceed with the matter, I intend now to place on the record exactly what is the situation. This article, which would be read extensively in western Canada where this subject is of utmost importance, contains statements to which I should like to refer, one being:
It is a curious fact that so far no party has advocated payment by the wheat board on the farm-that is, neither lending nor advancing money but making a partial payment on the farm.
Later in the same article these words appear:
The loans or advances proposed alike by the Liberal, Conservative and C.C.F. parties would be repayable by farmers in cash.
I realize that those who are dealing with the debates in this house must find it difficult to follow every detail, but most certainly this article is entirely inconsistent with the facts. For that reason, and because this subject is so important, it does become necessary to place side by side with that statement what has already been said, and said without any uncertainty. An added reason why this becomes necessary is that the Minister of Justice took it on himself to enlighten his own constituents by a letter to the Minnedosa Tribune. He was discussing this proposal by the government which is now under consideration. He tried to throw a smoke-screen around the debate that has been taking place here and he sought to convey an inaccurate impression of what has been said in this house. Whatever excuse may be offered on behalf of the writer of an article of this kind, such an excuse does not apply to a member of the house who sits here and knows perfectly well what the facts are. This statement was contained in the letter of the Minister of Justice to the Minnedosa Tribune:
This is a much more beneficial arrangement for western wheat farmers than any small difference there might be between bank loans at five per cent and a slightly lesser rate of interest on advances made by the wheat board.
IMr. Castleden.]
That is the line that is being followed in attempting to becloud the issue. The suggestion is being made and, undoubtedly, innocently picked up by others who are not so directly acquainted with the facts, that it is simply a difference of the method by which the loans will be advanced and repaid. That, of course, is not the situation. Not at the beginning of this debate, nor even during the recent months that have passed, but very much earlier, we advocated that there should be legislation on the statute books under which it would be possible to make cash payment for wheat stored on the farm at any time when the elevator space to absorb that wheat was not available. I made that specific proposal, as I have mentioned on other occasions, on December 17, 1952. I am not going to suggest that others may not have made that on earlier occasions. I do say it is a matter of record in Hansard that on December 17, 1952, I advocated without any reservation that there should be placed on the statute books legislation which would make it possible to pay cash for grain stored on the farm where that grain could not be taken over by the elevators which would ordinarily provide not only the storage but the payments.
I indicated then, as I have indicated since, that we are dealing with an abnormal situation and that the farmer has no place to look to but the government for the grain he produces, under the laws and regulations as they now stand. Because of the attempt to create the impression that it is only a question of which kind of loan and the amount of interest that is involved, it does become necessary to recall what has been said during this present session. The fact that it was said so short a time ago makes it doubly difficult to understand why anybody should be so confused about what has taken place in this house, and particularly a minister of the crown'who has been following a subject. This was what I said on January 12, 1956, and this session opened only on January 10. I quote from my remarks recorded at page 40 of Hansard:
The banks are not in a position to carry out any system of cash payments. There was a perfectly simple method, and that was to make cash payments as advances on the quota book in the ordinary way in relation to a stated quota of the grain grown last year, and then to have the grain made deliverable upon demand as soon as space became available in the elevators. No real difficulty presents itself in connection with that. The elevators are strategically situated to absorb the grain; the elevators have the staff to do the job. The elevators could have handled it satisfactorily under a system that would have been simple and that would have involved no serious difficulties of any kind.

Then I discussed the responsibilities of the government in regard to this matter, and on page 41 of Hansard I am reported as saying the following:
I have made certain proposals and I repeat them now. One: Provision should be made for immediate cash advances in the ordinary way on the quota book by the wheat board for farm-stored grain on a quota basis, making an initial payment thereon as if the wheat had been delivered to the elevator. The wheat would then be delivered on demand by the farmer as elevator space became available.
Two: Low-grade wheat now occupying elevator storage space while high-grade wheat cannot be stored should be sold for feed grain in Ontario, Quebec and abroad. This would provide elevator space for a good part of last year's high quality crop.
Three: The government should recruit top-flight salesmen from Canadian business concerns who would plan an aggressive selling policy for Canadian wheat and give advice as to long-term selling policies.
Four: The government should refer the whole problem of the handling and sale of Canadian wheat and its relationship to the Canadian economy as a whole to the Gordon commission on Canada's economic prospects and ask for an early interim report as well as a more complete report later on.
Five: The government should take immediate steps to assure the full use of all elevator space.
Those were the specific proposals made at that time. They were definite; they were clear; they were not subject to any qualifications. Since that time, in the discussion which has taken place, I have emphasized the vital importance of a statement by the government at this time as to what its policy is going to be, not only in regard to this immediate problem but in regard to the crop that will be grown in 1956. I have pointed out that not only are we concerned with the immediate and urgent problem confronting so many farmers in western Canada at this time but that these farmers very shortly will be called upon to ask themselves what they are going to do about seeding for the coming year. It is the duty, it is the urgent obligation of this government, not only to the farmers of western Canada but to all Canadians, to say now what they are going to do about the 1956 crops. Otherwise we may have a gravely aggravated situation infinitely worse even than that which exists today.
The government can have no excuse. Not only from ourselves but from members of other parties in this house, although not from the government side, has come the demand that there be a clear statement in regard to the policy that will govern our farmers in their seeding and in the planting of their crops for the current year.
Now I should like to deal with another matter. I pointed out that there is a vital and fundamental difference between this
Grain
problem and the problem that confronts many other agricultural producers. It is very natural for the potato grower in Prince Edward Island, in New Brunswick or elsewhere to say to himself that he faces an even more urgent problem. In some ways in regard to his own farming he does. He has a perishable crop. He has a crop that cannot be held in the same way. The farmer who is relying mainly on potatoes faces a real crisis. The same can be said of the apple grower. The same can be said of other agricultural producers. But I pointed out that there is a difference. These problems must be dealt with. It is the responsibility of the government to face up to these problems.
In the case of the western wheat grower, however, there is a particular aspect to the problem which makes it a different problem and one for which every member of parliament must accept responsibility. We are accepting that responsibility by urging the government to act now in a practical, sensible way in order to meet the immediate requirements and also to state their policy for the current year so that the farmers may know where they are at in planning their seeding for the current year.
We have also urged, as it is our duty to do, certain specific things with regard to the long term problem as well. In order that other Canadians not living in the prairie provinces and not directly affected by this may understand why this problem is different and why there is a special obligation on the part of the government to take appropriate steps with respect to the situation, I said this, as recorded at page 608 of Hansard of January 27 of this year:
One of the things which should be borne in mind, without in any way debating all the questions that may arise as to details of operation and otherwise, is the fact that the government says by law "this is our grain", which makes them in effect the owners of that grain the moment it is harvested.
I emphasize that point. In effect the moment the wheat is harvested the government becomes the owner of the grain. There is no other purchaser. The wheat farmer has been permitted to assume, and with reason, that the wheat would be taken up appropriately year by year so that from this grain, which must be delivered to the government agency, he would get an adequate return on the basis of a quota per acre at the initial price fixed by the board, and that this amount would then be handed to him as a cash advance on his quota book.
Our argument, and we have put it forward for some considerable time, not just in the last few months, is that the government alone can take the wheat and the government is already in fact the ultimate owner and by law can be the only owner in the end when it is sold.
That is the crux of this whole problem, Mr. Chairman. The government has said: You can only sell to us. The government has implied: You can look to us for an adequate

Grain
return. Any other interpretation would be meaningless, would be senseless. Unless and until the government is prepared to say that some other policy applies, it is reasonable for the farmers of western Canada to expect that they would get an appropriate cash payment for their grain. When the government has failed to take the necessary steps to clear the elevators, that is all the more reason why the government must provide a cash payment to the farmer on his farm for the grain which in fact can only be sold to the government.
It is not open to question that there is over 100 million bushels of elevator space in this country at the present time where grain could be absorbed if the government took real action with respect to this matter. It is not open to question that certain things could have been done under the authority of the government to move out lower quality grain and make way for the high quality grain which is marketable at all times with appropriate sales efforts in the markets of the world.
These are the things we have put before the house. I have only re-entered the discussion in the committee stage to correct the most inaccurate impression that was conveyed, I am sure innocently in the case of the writer of the Winnipeg Free Press but I am certain not so innocently by the Minister of Justice.

When the Minister of Trade and Commerce opened this debate, he spoke about the sales of wheat for the last five years and said there is no period of five years which comes within hundreds of millions of bushels of this record, and that is quite true.

However, the minister did not say that for the same period farm costs had been at the highest level of any time in the history of Canada. The minister indicated that he was very well satisfied with sales. I am sorry that he and the Minister of Agriculture do not agree, and I am sorry that he does not take time to read his own statistics.

The French grain board has made another large sale in the form of around 200,000 tons (7,349,000 bushels) of wheat and 100,000 tons of flour (5,062,000 bushels of wheat equivalent) to Poland. Recent purchases have been at $71.25 per ton ($1.94 per bushel) c.i.f. with a year's credit.
If France is prepared to make wheat available to Poland on that basis, then I do not think the minister should consider what he has proposed to do as a secret. If this type of transaction is to continue the minister is going to have to take the people of Canada into his confidence and encourage the purchase by Canadians of some of the goods that Poland must sell if it is to participate annually in this sort of transaction. It is not good enough for the minister to suggest that it is secret.
I understand that Poland wanted to buy
200,000	tons of wheat. I realize that the government must decide whether they can take a risk as to credit, but I should think that, with such large supplies of wheat on hand, having once decided that we will take some chances in extending credit, we should be ready to take further chances by extending additional credit. Nearly everyone in the west who wants to get something in the west can get it if wheat can be used on a barter basis. There is wheat all over the place and farmers are dealing with one another and making deals with the townspeople. Wheat is being used for a variety of purposes.
If Poland is prepared to take part of their imports from Canada we should welcome that sort of transaction. Apparently France has
Grain
agreed to give credit for a year for 7 million bushels in the form of wheat and over 5 million bushels in the form of flour. With such a large volume of wheat on hand I see no reason why we should not be prepared to extend more credit for a longer period.
I understand that Poland is making a real effort to get goods into this country. I have seen some of the booklets they are putting out on Polish foreign trade which are printed in English, French, German, Spanish and Russian. They are sending these out with a view to interesting Canadian importers and buyers in their products. I suggest that the two organizations with which I am associated, the wheat pool in Saskatchewan and the federated co-op, should be brought into the minister's confidence.
For instance, last fall you could not buy cement within 60 miles of where I live. Finally we were able to get hold of some United States cement but the price was 80 cents a bag more than Canadian cement. At the same time Poland was trying to get cement into the Canadian market. When we are unable to supply our own market it seems to me that the Department of Trade and Commerce should be-

I realize that in his opening statement the minister referred tc exports of wheat in a general way and a discussion of that kind is not being denied any hon. member during the course of this debate but I do feel that these particular matters have little or no relationship to the resolutior under discussion and therefore should not be entered into at this time.

speechtext: The hon. member who has interrupted me has not taken part in this debate but I am sure he will not go back to Swift Current-Maple Creek and try to convince the people there that this proposed legislation is good enough for the people of Canada.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, 1 am not going to traverse any of the ground that I covered on a previous occasion, but I do want to reiterate the stand I took against bank loans on the security of farmers' wheat. During the last few days, as a consequence of the debates that have taken place in this house, I find that western farmers more than ever regard this legislation as something in the nature of a deliberate slap at their legitimate demands. The hon. member who has just resumed his seat suggested to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that ministers of the cabinet, under the circumstances which he outlined, should be advised that instead of getting their monthly salary they might very well go to the bank and borrow. It occurs to me that there has been a great change in the Minister of Trade and Commerce in recent years. A few years ago he said, "What is a million?" But the other day he said, "I aim not interested in those who think $1,500 is chicken feed."

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: While we are on that subject may I say that a few years before that I was going to the bank to borrow money so I could pay the people who were employed by me.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am still comparing the million dollar mentality of the minister with bis later comment in regard to the farmers when he said that he was not interested in the man who thought that $1,500 as the maximum loan under this plan was chicken Eeed.
As far as the western farmer is concerned, be is not asking for a handout nor is he expecting to receive anything in the nature rf a handout under the legislation now before this house. The alternative suggested by the

opposition is a system of cash advances on wheat in the farmers' granaries.
Some mention was made the other day that the wheat pool of Saskatchewan was in favour of this legislation. 1 have before me a report which appeared in the Star-Phoenix of November 9 last in which it was indicated that the wheat pool officials, having read a report to the effect that the government bank loan policy was supported by the pool, issued the following statement:
Over the years, the policy of the wheat pool organization is laid down by the delegates in annual meeting . . . After a very complete discussion of the whole situation, the delegates passed resolutions, reading as follows:
"That we urge the government of Canada to make immediate provision for advances to farmers on farm-stored grain.
"That advances to farmers on farm-stored grain should be up to one-half the normal delivery expected and repayable on the basis of one-half of the value of each delivery made by the farmer.
"That advances on farm-stored grain should be made by way of government-guaranteed loans to the Canadian wheat board; the Canadian wheat board to arrange with elevator companies to make the advances to individual farmers, and that any interest involved in such loans should be absorbed by the federal treasury."
That in general represents the viewpoint not only of the wheat pool organization in Saskatchewan but of farmers in general throughout the province. The situation in which they find themselves today is resulting in very pronounced reductions in the purchases by farmers of those manufactured products which come into the western provinces, in the main, from the eastern provinces. This is not a sectional problem. This is a national problem, the maintenance of a fair purchasing power among farmers.
The other day mention was made of the prices of wheat during the 1930's as compared with today, to indicate that today there was no real need for cash advances. What really counts is the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat. According to unchallengeable statistics issued by the bureau of statistics, it is interesting to note that the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat of the 1953-54 crop is the same as the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat in 1933-34. In other words the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat today, as then, is 70 cents. In 1934-35-that would be the period while Mr. Bennett was in power-the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat was 84 cents. Then that figure went up and down, and last year we found-and the situation is worse this year-that the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat was 70 cents. It was 71 cents in 1939-40. It rose to $1.28 in 1945-46; the purchasing price since 1945-46 until 1954 has fallen by 58 cents to the bushel. That is a major consideration. It

is not the actual price; it is what that price will supply in purchasing power.
When I hear my hon. friends opposite talking about the 1930's, let me repeat this. In 1953-54 the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat was exactly the same as it was in 1933-34. That, I hope, is an answer to the situation of the western farmer. It is less today. The purchasing power of the 1954-55 and 1955-56 bushel of wheat today is approximately 59 cents a bushel. In other words it is much lower than it was in 1933 and 1934, which indicates the major need for something to be done.
As far as this present plan is concerned, I do not know anybody who is in favour of it outside of this house and other than Liberal supporters in the country who, regardless of what the government does, support it. Even in the last few days one or two organizations have passed resolutions in support of this policy of advances on grain in the granaries. The Saskatchewan credit union league, in the last 10 days or so, passed a resolution in support of it. So, generally speaking, the farmers are asking for a very simple action on the part of this government.
There is no danger of loss. Any suggestion that fraud will be committed is denied by the fact that the local elevator man in each case knows approximately the production of all the farmers in his area. The quota book hampers any possibility of wrongdoing among the small percentage of wrongdoers. Indeed, a few years ago there used to be a great many wheat thefts. There are no wheat thefts any more because there is no quota book for thieves, and there is no way in which a thief can in any way dispose of wheat that does not belong to him.
I mentioned a moment ago the decline in the purchasing power of wheat. Now I wish to refer to the price of Canadian wheat in the free market. I am quoting from the representations Dr. Britnell made last June. He is head of the department of economics of the University of Saskatchewan. He says the price of Canadian wheat in the free market has fallen almost 50 cents a bushel over the past two years.

I really cannot understand my hon. friends from the western provinces who support the government in the face of this almost universal demand, believing that haphazard dibs and dabs here and there will meet the situation.
The other day the minister provided for a payment of 10 cents a bushel on certain grades of the 1954-55 crop. As far as northern Saskatchewan is concerned, and I am speaking now of the Prince Albert district, the Prince Albert Herald immediately recorded the fact in its news columns that almost all the wheat in that area graded lower than 4 and that therefore the advance of 10 cents a bushel, welcome as it was-and I welcomed it when it was made the other day-will not help those farmers whose crop is grade 5, 6 or feed. I suggest to the minister that something be done to extend the application of the advance of 10 cents a bushel; otherwise it will be of no advantage to farmers in many parts of northern Saskatchewan.
As far as the policy contemplated by the resolution is concerned, it does not, it cannot and it will not meet the situation. It constitutes a stubborn and relentless disregard of the wishes of the people. It seems almost as if the government has determined that they have a steamroller majority, and regardless of the wishes of the western farmers they are going to push the measure through hoping that by the time the next election comes around something will happen that will cause the western farmers to forget. There will be no forgetfulness, Mr. Chairman, of this deliberate slap in the face to the western farmer.
This is something that could be repaired even at this time. With all its power the government finally abdicated last summer from the arrogance of the position it took on the Defence Production Act. It is not too late now for the government to take action, realizing the universal demand for cash advances on farm-stored grain is supported not only by all the farmers but also by the

opposition parties in the house and by many of my hon. friends who support the government who, were they able to speak as they feel, would denounce this resolution as unjust to the legitimate demands of western Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the members of the government may wonder why they are meeting such opposition in introducing this measure at this time. I think I can offer some explanation of that; the method by which they introduced it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce stated in a previous debate that before going out to address the annual convention of the Saskatchewan wheat pool he knew that things were rather bad and something would have to be done, so he introduced the bank loan legislation. It is a very ill-conceived piece of legislation, because it does not take into consideration the wishes and desires of the farmers and farm organizations in western Canada. It is ill-conceived because of the way it was introduced, by order in council and by a television program.
It seems to me that we in this democratic parliament are receiving an annual stipend commensurate with a year's work, and I think we should be free at all times to be called together to discuss such important problems. Had we been granted that privilege the Minister of Trade and Commerce would have had our advice expressing the views of the farmers and farm organizations in our constituencies, and he would have been able to modify the resolution in conformity with our suggestions in order to meet the requests of western Canadian farmers.
He could, for example, have taken into consideration the resolutions which the hon. member for Rosthern continually ignores in all his dissertations. The hon. member for Rosthern tries very hard to prove that a bank loan is a cash advance or vice versa. He has quoted at length from the conference held in Saskatoon. I should like to read certain resolutions passed on the first day of the 31st annual convention of the Saskatchewan wheat pool after the suspension of the regular order of business. These resolutions were passed virtually unanimously on the floor of the assembly. They are under the heading, "Advances on farm-stored grain", and read as follows:
2.	That we urge the government of Canada to make immediate provision for advances to farmers on farm-stored grain.
3.	That advances to farmers on farm-stored grain should be up to one-half the normal delivery expected and repayable on the basis of one-half of the value of each delivery made by the farmer.
4.	That advances on farm-stored grain should be made by way of government guaranteed loans to

the Canadian wheat board; the Canadian wheat board to arrange with elevator companies to make the advances to individual farmers; and further, that any interest involved in such loans should be absorbed by the federal treasury.
That is quite a different thing from the proposal already conceived by those in the higher brackets of the government before going out to discuss the problem at the Saskatchewan wheat pool convention.
The subdistrict and district conventions of the Saskatchewan farmers' union could have given the minister some valuable advice and recommendations. If the minister had doubted their capacity to represent the farmers he could have asked the municipal councils, and there would have been no doubt left whatsoever as to the inadequacy of government guaranteed bank loans on the basis of the 1951 legislation. He could have gone further and asked individual farmers. Individual farmers I have asked indicated to me that they were unalterably opposed to the principle of paying interest on their own money. As a result of the meetings held in the constituency last fall I have concluded that we could sum up this legislation by saying that it is unjust, inadequate and impracticable. It has been pointed out by my colleagues that it is unjust because it requires farmers to borrow money on their own earnings.
There are many members of this house who have no comprehension whatsoever of the conditions that exist in agriculture in western Canada. It is most sickening to hear members talk about western farmers driving about in their Cadillacs. The hon. member for Westmorland gave an indication of that lack of knowledge on the part of members from other parts of Canada. Their absence at the vote last Friday indicated that they were not concerned with the problem. In fact, as I recall it the hon. member for Westmorland served on the agriculture committee. In order to impress him with the importance of our task, I took him down a sample of wheat. He greeted me with thanks, saying that he had never seen it before. What kind of advice can we expect from members who have no knowledge of the subject matter and who are not interested in finding out?

As was pointed out by my colleagues, this legislation is unjust because the financial position of the farmers in western Canada demands that they have additional purchasing power with which to pay off previous commitments such as store bills, gasoline bills and labour charges incurred during the harvesting season. In many
Grain
instances they are unable to borrow directly from the bank. They were unable to sell their grain. The crux of the matter really is that of correcting the cost-price relationship of the farmers with respect to the goods they are obliged to buy and the prices they receive for their products. It is indeed a cruel blow to see a surcharge of 5 per cent placed on the moneys to which the farmers are entitled.
I say the resolution is most inadequate because, as the hon. member for Prince Albert has pointed out, the minister said he was not interested in the farmer who thought $1,500 was chicken feed. I think the minister would do well to refer to some of the publications put out by his colleague the Minister of Agriculture, because in the Economic Annalist of February, 1951, there is a study on costs of farming in the Elbow-Saskatoon area of Saskatchewan in 1948-49. Since 1951 it is estimated that the cost of production has increased by 20 per cent. It therefore works out, Mr. Chairman, in this way. The costs of production on a one-section farm in the Saskatoon-Elbow area, on good soil, were $2,006 in 1948-49. Costs have increased nearly 20 per cent since that time, so the cost in 1955 would be over $2,400. By the same token, the costs of production on a larger farm, one of over 800 acres, would be nearly $4,000. These are the cash outlays required to operate your farm. The minister must reorganize his thinking. He must appreciate the fact that was pointed out by my leader in the previous debate, namely that the purchasing power of a bushel of wheat has declined 50 per cent since 1945.
The Canada Year Book points out that in 1955 Saskatchewan had 247 branch banks, Alberta had 270 and Manitoba had 175. This problem is a real one in my constituency. For example, there is a bank in the town of Leader. If someone in the area of Horsham down in the southwest corner of my constituency is desirous of going to the bank to get this loan, he must travel 55 miles to go to the bank. He normally does his business with the credit union in Fox Valley, but this legislation requires him to go to a bank. He will therefore make the trip to the bank and make application for the loan. He will fill out the necessary forms and return to his farm.
The banker will have the task of mulling over the application. He has never seen the farmer before. He does not know whether the farmer has on his farm 1,000 bushels of wheat or 1,000 head of sheep or just 1,000 trees. So when it comes to a matter of resolving the question of granting the loan, knowing that bankers are in this business for the purpose

I have placed a question on the order paper to determine the amount and the number of these loans but evidently I do not have the same luck in getting this information as does the Minister of Agriculture, since the question as yet is unanswered.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the case for the western farmer has been so well put by so many able speakers on the opposition side this afternoon that I believe it would be impossible for me to say anything that would not be a repetition of what has already been said. In the circumstances I think I will not say a great many of the things I had intended to say. But, in discussing the resolution calling for provision for making loans to western farmers, what actually is being done is something like this. The measure provides for only a nibble at a slice, while the wheat grower is entitled to, and ought to be granted, the whole loaf of bread. He has earned it; he ought to have it.
Everywhere on the prairies we have the demand for advances on farm-stored grain. This demand comes from all over the west. Apparently the government has made up its mind that in spite of everything it will not give the western farmers, or the western provinces, what they want.
This measure reminds me of a few words which I read from Nikita Khrushchev's remarks last September. He said:
If you really think (addressing the capitalist world) that your system is not too old and rotten, if you believe that it is really possible to keep in the race, go ahead and try and compete. But the truth is on the side of our people.
If Khrushchev wanted a specific instance to establish the general truth of his position, le could ask for nothing any better than this lontemptible wheat loan proposal the govern-nent is offering to the farmers of western Canada. Here we have Canada one of the inest capitalist nations of the earth, endowed vith about the finest resources to be found n the world, with a production of over $26 iillion in the year just past, showing abund-intly that it is completely possible physically o provide those farmers with all they want. U1 that is required is a little financial intelli-;ence to make financially possible what is ihysically possible-and here we have the ibsolutely disgusting scene which is presented >y Canada at the present time! I must say am absolutely ashamed of the government. In my speech of January 13 I advocated immediate payment on wheat stored on farms o cover full average costs of production, plus living allowance large enough to cover the 
average costs of carrying on. My remarks are to be found on page 95 of Hansard. That is all we want, and certainly that is what we ought to get.
I will quote a statement from the caucus of the Social Credit members of Alberta, which will show the position they took after the proposal was made to make available loans of up to $1,500 at 5 per cent. I am quoting from one of the Alberta newspapers:
The federal government program of loans to farmers on farm-stored grain Wednesday was described as "entirely inadequate" by Social Credit members of the legislature attending their annual fall caucus in Edmonton.
The policy statement on the wheat situation said, "The proposal to put farmers further in debt is unfair and unjust."
It added, "Not many farmers will be able to qualify for the full amount of the loan. Even if more of them did, the amount would not be sufficient in many cases to take care of the debts incurred in putting in and taking out the crop.
We believe the federal government should make it possible for the Canadian wheat board to make cash advances to the farmers against grain stored on the farms. The Canadian government should make an immediate start on provisions of approved storage on the farms.
One way of doing this would be to pay the farmers storage rates on the same basis paid to elevators, if they built approved storage facilities.
It is obvious the federal government does not* have the answer to surplus production. We do not look upon surpluses as a calamity. It is only when we bungle the handling of them that they become such. If we provide proper storage, widely dispersed on the farms, and are prepared to use the national credit to finance the cash advance against the surpluses so stored, these surpluses can become a blessing to our country, and the world in the years ahead".
I think nothing more needs to be said by me. The hon. member for Prince Albert presented a case which, as far as I could see, was as completely airtight as it could be, a case which makes utterly contemptible the efforts of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture to becloud the issue and confuse the people generally by playing a lot of silly, childish politics when they should have been facing up like responsible members of the cabinet of Canada and dealing with the problem honourably and honestly.
Just as an example of some of the things the two right hon. gentlemen have attempted to convey-I hope I am not unfair-the first point was that there would be greater costs in the case of advances than there would be under the loans which Eire proposed. The case made by the hon. member for Prince Albert explodes that idea completely. Surely the government of the Dominion of Canada, with all the credit behind it of this great nation, could borrow money in a vast sum incomparably more cheaply than could any farmer, even though the government's guarantee is behind his loan.

If the money were borrowed in a large lump sum and advanced to the wheat board, with instructions that the wheat board would disperse that money or disperse it through the elevators to the farmers, you would have none of the costs that were conjured up by some of the speakers on the other side as being certain to accrue if advances were offered to farmers.
The argument that this process would wreck the wheat board is absolutely puerile.
I do not know how a man could undertake to delude the Canadian people in that way, how he could stand up and face a parliament of intelligent people or go out and address an intelligent audience, and say it could possibly wreck the wheat board to take a vast sum of money borrowed by the dominion government from the Bank of Canada, put into the wheat board's hands and dispensed through the elevators to the farmers as a forward payment or an advance payment on farm-stored grain. How that could wreck the wheat board it would require a congregation of lunatics to see. There just is no sense at all in such a position. Apparently a deliberate attempt was made to confuse the people of Canada through the press from coast to coast into believing this bit of nonsense.
An attempt was made to indicate that the farmers were fairly well off. These hon. gentlemen were not able to find very many farmers who were sufficiently in need to have any requirement for advances! That is almost in the class with the other piece-I must keep from using too strong words-of nonsense, I will say once more. If in the United States, just across the border, farmers can store grain on their farms and get $2.10 per bushel; if in the United States farmers are fairly well off, how can it be reasoned that Canadian farmers on this side of the border, under the treatment that has been meted out to them, can be said to be fairly well off, especially when it is remembered that the costs of producing in Canada are just as great as they are in the United States, if not greater.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is with great difficulty that I approach this subject with coolness, owing to the fact that we are discussing a resolution to bring in an innocuous bill in respect to bank loans to wheat farmers. I feel that this government is to be sharply criticized for its inaction in meeting the situation that has developed in western Canada. It was certainly plain to all people who at least wanted to explore the situation that there was difficulty in respect to the grain marketing situation in western Canada, and in respect to the western farmer's income.
I may say, in spite of the optimism the Minister of Trade and Commerce expressed in this house on occasions during the latter part of the last session, that some of us, particularly in this group, indicated to him that we had great concern about the movement of grain in this country and the plight of western farmers, and we tried to bring to the attention of this government the fact that a real policy for agriculture was needed to meet the ever-growing surpluses of grain in this country. I wrote the Prime Minister on October 3, 1955, before the crop season, and urged that consideration be given to an immediate plan of cash advances to farmers on farm-stored grain. The premier of Saskatchewan also, in view of the situation which he knew was developing, sent a telegram to the Prime Minister on October 24, which reads as follows:
Saskatchewan government feels that proposed bank loans on farm-stored grain will not meet present situation. Urge that cash advances be handled by the Canadian wheat board through elevator companies. Farmers of this province almost unanimously in favour of cash advances through wheat board as permanent feature of orderly marketing system. Strenuous objection being taken by farmers to proposed bank loans on farm-stored grain as being unsatisfactory method of meeting present critical situation.
I want to indicate some of the factors leading up to the present situation. I may say that some of the western newspapers came to the rescue of the farmers in their effort to depict the situation to this indifferent government. I should like to refer to the questionnaire distributed by the Saskatchewan Farmer and Livestock Times as reported in their publication of November 3. With respect to the questionnaire it has this to say:
Nearly 56 per cent favoured direct cash advances on farm-stored grain as a means of getting immediate cash into the hands of the farmers while just under 13 per cent recommended low interest loans.
Almost without exception the western farm organizations have been in favour of cash advances, interest free, on farm-stored grain.
I for one do not feel that the measure before us will meet the situation adequately at all.

I believe that the provision of bank loans, with the banks having the right to charge 5 per cent interest, is nothing short of a farce as far as meeting the needs of the western farmers is concerned. Indeed, it is more than that; it is an insult to the western farmer who obtains his income from the production of wheat and now, by reason of this iniquitous legislation, is forced because of the market situation to go to the banks in order to get cash with which to meet his obligations.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture are to be sharply criticized for the statements they have made in and out of the house respecting the financial position of western farmers. I have here the issue of the Western Producer of February 2, which deals with an earlier statement carried in the Globe and Mail of January 24. The Globe and Mail article is headed, "Gardiner argues income up and farmers not badly off." The article in the Western Producer refers to a statement made at the meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture held in Hamilton, and it is headed, "Making monkeys out of us, delegate criticizes Gardiner."
I feel there has been a definite underhand movement on the part of government officials to try to play down the present critical cash situation facing western farmers. I believe the present position, as it has developed, is even worse than that. In my opinion members of the house are now being intimidated by the attempt of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to use what is termed in one editorial "shotgun methods" to squelch any opposition in the house to the government's proposed bank loans.
I have here an article that appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of February 6, 1956. It quotes Hansard and goes on to say that Mr. Howe foresaw a filibuster. At another point in the article it has this to say:
He insisted that the highly unpopular bank loans bill must be approved before the storage bill can be considered. In his words, "We have undertaken to pass a very simple resolution and until that is passed we are not prepared to take any other resolution." He has thus, in effect, made consideration of a final payment on 1954-55 deliveries dependent on the passage of the loans legislation-a bill that has nothing whatsoever to do with wheat payments. Mr. Howe's desire to get this unpopular legislation through the house with a minimum of embarrassment to the government is quite understandable. Western farmers, however, would have more confidence in the legislation- and in the minister-if he did not apparently feel it necessary to use shotgun methods to secure parliament's approval of it.
I for one want to say that as far as I am concerned there is going to be no intimidation of me in this house at any time, and I speak for 98 per cent of the western farmers when

I say they are unalterably opposed to bank loans and paying interest on their own grain. I am one who has great faith in democracy, perhaps more than is indicated sometimes by the actions we see on the other side of the house. This afternoon I heard the Minister of Justice quoted as having said at a meeting in his own province that there were two methods, the first being bank loans through the banks at 5 per cent interest and the second loans at perhaps a lesser rate of interest from the Canadian wheat board.
I think the Minister of Justice should confer with his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that if the Canadian wheat board were to undertake what we are proposing as an alternative method of giving advances to the farmers it would wreck the wheat board. Now the Minister of Justice says it will not wreck it but just partially destroy it. He has not suggested in his statement by any means that the Canadian wheat board could not have handled this matter.
Therefore I think the whole thing is a phony issue when the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Agriculture or anyone else suggests that it is not possible for the federal government to authorize the wheat board to make cash advances to the farmers interest free. We now see the Minister of Trade and Commerce trying to use dire threats in order to prevent members putting the real situation before the house.
The key problem has not developed overnight but over the years. It has only come to the fore because the cost-price squeeze has now developed to a point where the farmer is left without any cash in his hands. It is true that over the last five years we have had unprecedented production of grain in western Canada, but it is also true that the income of the western farmer has dropped very substantially, particularly in the last three years. I should like to give the house the bureau of statistics figures showing the drop in farm cash income in the province of Saskatchewan for the nine month period beginning in January and ending in September in the years 1953, 1954 and 1955. In 1955 the figure was $305 million. In 1954 it was $300-2 million and in 1953 it was $516-7 million.
There we have the story. From $516-7 in 1953 there has been a drop to $305 million in 1955. In addition, the Minister of Agriculture is prone to refer only to the cash income of the western farmer. He nearly always fails-as a matter of fact I have never heard him do it-to give the net income to the western farmer. In other words he gives the cash picture, but he does not give the net
Grain
income to the western farmer; and relatively speaking, net income is the real income.

speechtext:
As I
indicated earlier, because of the heavy crops this drastic situation which has now developed in western Canada did not come to the fore. So in 1951 agricultural prices were at 268-7 and costs were at 225-5. But by 1954 agricultural prices had deteriorated to 200 * 9 and costs had increased to 234 [DOT] 4. It is therefore understandable how the farmers have come to a cash position where they cannot pay their debts, and where they now should and must have some cash income to make up for their inability to deliver their grain in order to pay their debts.
As I said before, I am quite happy that some of the newspapers have taken it upon themselves to help to present to the Canadian people the actual financial position facing western farmers. That information can be found by the government if they want to read some of these newspapers. I have here an

Grain
article appearing in the Toronto Star. It is a dispatch written by correspondent Robert Nielsen who, I understand, has written a series of articles. He has toured the west; he has gone into Saskatchewan and some of the other provinces and obtained firsthand information as to just what is the situation. I want to read from this article. He is talking about the bumper crops and the present situation. He says:
That ailment is a cost-price squeeze. Between 1951 and 1954 the Saskatchewan prices of farm products (at the farm) fell by nearly 25 per cent while the prices of the goods and services the farmer buys rose by nearly 5 per cent.
Then he goes on to show that in the bountiful years between 1951 and 1954 the farmer was getting by but that now the cost-price squeeze has caught up with him. In the same article it is indicated that Professor K. A. H. Buckley scored the Ottawa government, and I quote:
. . . for not having developed a grain storage policy to accompany the price stabilization policy effected by the wheat board.
I speak for myself, and I think for this group, when I say we support the wheat board's policy of marketing grain. Here is a situation where the farmer, after producing his grain, must depend upon this government and its policy to sell that wheat for him in order to receive his income. This government is now bringing in and forcing on this house the present legislation which will compel the farmer, if he wants any cash from his wheat, to go to the bank and pay bank interest.
I have in mind another resolution and, I suppose, legislation which will come before this house where a certain corporation will be given a low rate of interest on a projected pipe line. Here we have the farmer who has produced his wheat, who now, like any other person with an income in this country, must go through a great deal of processing, must give certain details of his financial status, and take out bank loans at 5 per cent interest. As far as I am concerned that is nothing short of adding insult to injury.
Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, I had a return tabled in the house which shows that this government is not doing its job and that the eternal optimism of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is often misleading. I am speaking now with respect to the marketing of wheat in this country. He assured the farmers last year that their bins would be empty and that they would be able to sell their wheat.
I had a question on the order paper and I obtained a return as to the trade commissioners in foreign countries and how many of those were specifically appointed

to sell Canadian wheat. The return I received on January 24 states that out of 85 trade commissioners posted in 55 places, not one is specifically appointed to sell Canadian wheat. When wheat is our primary industry, I feel that we certainly should have some people appointed to go abroad and try to find markets for that wheat. Thus we have the situation backing up on us, and now the farmer once again is going to be obliged to stand the brunt of it.
I never felt at any time that bank loans were going to meet the situation. I wrote to all the secretaries of the rural municipalities in my constituency and asked them for a survey of the financial situation of the farmers. In every case there has been growing arrears of taxes in all those municipalities. In addition, in one letter there is a comment in respect to bank loans. This secretary informs me that at this point, where there is a bank which serves not only that village but also three hamlets, to date only one bank loan has been issued.
I want to be fair in this matter, and say that this situation has arisen in a place where the farmers' crops have been fairly well drowned out because of the heavy rains and flood conditions last year. But the same fact remains, namely that here is a community which is similar to many others, where there has been only one bank loan issued up to date. I feel that this legislation does not meet the situation that prevails in western Canada.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce tried to indicate in this house that those of us who are unalterably opposed to this resolution preceding a bill providing for the making of bank loans at 5 per cent interest are in effect trying to wreck the Canadian wheat board. Nothing could be more ridiculous or further from the truth. We support the Canadian wheat board. But if the western farmer is to have faith in the marketing of his wheat through the Canadian wheat board, we feel that this government has to wake up and has to formulate policies which will meet the situation.
I recall that last year one of the newspapers in my constituency carried an article which indicated that if we had a crop failure it perhaps would be a blessing in disguise. I believe that must be what this government is hoping for because of its failure to formulate policies to meet a situation where we are having great overproduction. I think, Mr. Chairman, that in the years to come we are going to have a situation where science and technology will help us produce more grain. I think we should be prepared for it.
I came into this house in 1945, and I have repeated the suggestion many times in the

house that we should adopt a policy of an ever-normal granary. I know that perhaps it is not an original suggestion. I said that I believed Canada should store grain in years of plenty to prepare for years of scarcity. I was only young during the thirties, but I recall that we were scraping our bins as we did not have any wheat. I believe it would be a good idea for the federal government to finance a policy under which this country would store wheat and other things for years of scarcity which have prevailed in the past and which undoubtedly will come again.
If we undertook such a policy, Mr. Chairman, we would not have this type of legislation coming before us which only puts the farmer in a more difficult financial position. We would set up a proper plan for agriculture whereby we would store for the years of scarcity. If we undertook such a plan I believe we could keep in federal storage the 400 million bushels of wheat which we need for domestic and export trade. We could do better than that, even. If our farm people could produce sufficient grain to carry a billion bushels of wheat in this country in government storage, it would be one of the greatest things for the peace of the world and security at home. The farmers would be paid for their grain and the grain would belong to the Canadian people.
Some of the newspapers have stated that there has been no definite statement as to what the opposition parties would propose as an alternative to bank loans. I do not feel that is a true statement, because those of us in this group who have spoken have made our position quite clear. We are against bank loans at 5 per cent interest. We do not believe it is fair. It is just as unreasonable as saying to the wage earner, you cannot get your wages but we will make arrangements with the bank to make you a loan on your income at 5 per cent interest. It is an analogous situation. We do not go along with the government's proposal. In this case we believe there should be a long and a shortterm policy undertaken. The government has allowed things to dangle along and get completely out of hand.
As an immediate solution I feel the government should have done what the farm organizations in Saskatchewan and in the west generally advocated, namely made cash advances on farm-stored grain through the Canadian wheat board. It would have been a very simple matter to put cash into the hands of the farmers, which would have enabled them to carry on until future deliveries took place. I am at a loss to know whether once again the government is trying to do a favour for the banks, or whether they
Grain
are not ready to undertake their responsibility as a government and underwrite a parity policy for all agricultural products.
This afternoon, Mr. Chairman, I heard a member from the province of New Brunswick state that the farmers in his constituency had never asked for handouts or for any bank loans. Well, I do not know what assistance they get down there, but I am one who has always favoured any policy which will help agriculture in every province and the people in every province, regardless of their occupation. I believe we in this house should realize that we are like the mother of parliaments, responsible for all the provinces. We should legislate to bring those policies into being which will be in the best interests of every Canadian, regardless of where he lives or what his occupation may be.
Getting back directly to the proposals, I would suggest first that this government should not introduce this legislation at this time. I feel it could do something better. The government could pay the interest on those loans already made, and then set up proper lending facilities through which the farmer could get interest free loans on farm-stored grain until such time as he could deliver his grain.
From time to time we have suggested tha1 this situation would not have developed ii the government had done certain things Amongst those suggestions has been bilateral agreements with other countries that would enable us to sell our wheat for the goods we wanted from the other countries. We have suggested barter arrangements. We have suggested the extension of credit. We have suggested that further assistance be giver under the Colombo plan, and also that in some cases famine relief be considered as a measure for helping people less fortunate than we
Another thing I want to deal with at an other time but which I should like to mentioi now is the tariff. I feel that a change in rate! would be of great assistance to the westeri farmer. speechtext:
It seems to me that a word now to bring this debate back into focus would be worth while. There seems to be a feeling on the opposite side that we are forcing something on the opposition. We are not doing that. At the request of the delegation that came down from western Canada, we arranged with the banks to institute a system of loans on farm storage grain. We thought we were following the wishes of the delegation that put this before us. The unfortunate thing is that the house not being in session, the government gave an undertaking to the banks that if they would not wait for legislation, as the first bill before this parliament the government would undertake to ratify the action it was asking the banks to take. In other words we asked them to lend money on the undertaking that the government would see that the losses were guaranteed.
Well, we have been a long time on this debate. I think most members in the C.C.F. party from the prairies have now spoken twice. I am willing to delay this matter. We will have to tell the banks we cannot carry out our undertaking now. We will have to tell them that at the end of the session we will undertake to keep the house here until we can have this undertaking by the government ratified. It will be up to the banks whether they want to continue lending without the guarantee, but the government is not insisting that this be thrust upon the farmers. We thought it would be helpful.
According to the records I have in hand, it has helped some 8,000 farmers. I have received some letters saying that they are eery happy with the assistance they have received. But somehow or other this has got iwisted around so that the government is attempting to force this policy on the opposition. It is nothing of the kind. It seems to me that no more repetitive speeches are leeded. We have had the same speeches made twice now, I think, by all the members :rom the prairies. I now see a member getting ip to speak for the third time. That is his privilege in committee; nevertheless, we are low down to the point of obstruction.
When we recall that this is a bill that can ie obstructed on second reading and on third [DOT]eading, as well as in the resolution stage, we [DOT]ealize that it is nothing new. There is lothing to debate in the principle of this bill, t is up to the opposition to decide whether hey want to carry this on tomorrow. I am villing to drop it until June, but it is just as he opposition say. I think there is a limit

to patience. When we get away from debate and get down to obstruction, I think I should have the privilege of making these remarks.

Interest has been expressed in this measure throughout the prairies. Hon. members have attended meetings called by the farmers' union groups and other groups throughout the prairies. If there is a great deal of interest evinced in this house it is certainly not out of proportion to the interest throughout the country.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce rose in his place in the house to answer a question asked by an hon. gentleman on the orders of the day just a few days ago and implied that there was a filibuster because we had had the temerity to debate this thing for one-half a day. If that is the attitude of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on a matter which has aroused the interest-and I might say the resentment-of farmers throughout the prairies, then I suggest the government know full well we are not getting the type of legislation which we have a right to expect.
I attended a few meetings and spoke to a great many farmers in southern Manitoba last fall. I found wherever I went great interest among the farmers and hostility and resentment toward this measure. We came down here. We are expected to put forth the views of our people, and we are not going to be intimidated by any minister of the crown.
Why the impatience? I suggest the minister is impatient to ram this through the house because he knows it is the most unpopular measure that has been brought before this house for some time. Because it is unpopular the government wishes to spare itself the embarrassment of criticism. You follow that

line of reasoning to its logical conclusion and it will lead you to a totalitarian state. Any time ministers rise in their places and suggest that the opposition are obstructionists because they wish to debate a measure, you get a scene such as we have had here today.
As far as the members of the government are concerned, they would just as soon the opposition did not say anything. They would like to be given a free hand to mismanage the country as they have done in the past.
I believe that the unseemly haste, the impatience of the minister in this connection, prove very revealingly the arrogance which we have been subjected to in the past. It reveals, I think, better than anything else the knowledge on the part of the government that this measure is highly unpopular. We have heard hon. members read the names of farm organizations throughout the prairies that have expressed their opposition to the measure.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

In spite of the fact that farm organizations and important people throughout the western prairies have protested against the measure, the government not only want to put it through, but they want to put it through with a minimum of discussion. I suggest that in a democratic parliament every member ought to have the right to speak his mind on any piece of legislation before the house.
A few moments ago the minister said that some members of this group had spoken two or three times. That is not true. There is not a member in this group who has spoken twice on this measure. I challenge the minister to name one. He cannot do it. Yet the minister suggested-he did not suggest it, he said it a moment ago-that a member of this group was getting up for the third time. That is patently false. I think it is time the minister pulled in his horns and permitted the opposition to do the job they were sent down here to do.
There is a resolution on the order paper dealing with farm storage. We were told in
Grain
effect by the minister the other day that he was not going to allow that matter to come before the house until he had rammed this bank loan resolution through. What happened? The other day we had an amazing spectacle. There were only 36 Liberals in the house, and when a vote was called on a motion for the committee to rise and report progress, and that motion was passed, we went on with the storage resolution. But the minister was not satisfied. Just as soon as he could round up enough of his cohorts he reverted to the bank loan legislation.
The country ought to know-indeed they do know-that the reason the storage legislation has not been passed at this time is entirely the responsibility of the government. The matter was brought before the committee, but because the minister was so angry and in a huff, and wanted to save face, he came back to this house and overrode the previous decision of the committee, disposing of the storage bill and turning back the committee to the bank loan legislation.
The fault is definitely with the government. I hope we hear no talk among the Liberals that the C.C.F. group have obstructed the legislation. I hope we will not have the Liberals going out saying they were anxious to pass the resolution and get this storage bill through, but the C.C.F. stood in the way. It is the government that has prevented the measure from coming up. As a matter of fact it was before the committee, but was turned aside in order that we could go back to this unpopular, controversial legislation.
Of course, we know from experience their efforts to use this kind of intimidation on the opposition to force it into silence.
Will you call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
Progress reported.
